concept.name: Yield-curve inversion
concept.definition: A condition in which short-term Treasury yields exceed long-term yields, inverting the normally upward-sloping term structure of interest rates. The Federal Reserve Bank of New York measures the term spread as the 10-year minus 3-month Treasury rate and uses its slope to estimate the probability of a recession twelve months ahead.
concept.intuition: Inversion signals that markets expect the central bank to cut rates because of coming weakness, so a negative spread has preceded nearly every modern U.S. recession with few false alarms.
concept.mechanics: Policy tightening pushes short rates above long rates, turning the term spread negative. The New York Fed feeds the monthly 10-year/3-month spread into a probit model that outputs the probability of recession within twelve months, publishing updates in the first two weeks of each month.
concept.formula: Term spread = Yield(10-year Treasury) - Yield(3-month Treasury); the curve is inverted when the spread is below zero.
concept.failure_modes: Lead times are long and variable - historically many months to around two years - and structural forces such as QE, compressed term premia, and foreign demand for long bonds can invert the curve without a near-term recession.
concept.misconceptions: Inversion is a probabilistic signal, not a mechanical cause of recession; the signal is considered more reliable when the curve stays inverted, and the New York Fed stresses its estimates are not official Federal Reserve forecasts.
concept.example: The 10-year/3-month spread turned negative in 2019 and again from late 2022 through 2024, reaching roughly -1.8 percentage points in mid-2023, the deepest inversion since the early 1980s.

citations.source: Federal Reserve Bank of New York, The Yield Curve as a Leading Indicator
